nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.7
nodes.statement: Let $Z_n$ denote the number of retained level-$n$ cubes after iteration step $n$ and set $Z_0:=1$. Since the retention probabilities $p_n$ vary with $n$, the process $(Z_n)_{n \geq 1}$ is a so-called branching process in a time-varying environment. Following the notation of Lyons in \cite{Lyo} let $L_n$ be a random variable, having the distribution of $Z_n$ given that $Z_{n-1}=1$. Note that $L_n$ has a binomial distribution with parameters $N^{d}$ and $p_{n}$. Define the process $(W_n)_{n \geq 1}$ by \[ W_n := \frac{Z_n}{\prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i N^d}. \] It is straightforward to show that $(W_n)_{n \geq 1}$ is a martingale: \begin{eqnarray*} \ensuremath{\mathbb{E}}[W_n | W_{n-1}] &=&\frac{\ensuremath{\mathbb{E}}[Z_n | Z_{n-1}]}{\prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i N^d} = \frac{Z_{n-1}}{\prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i N^d} \ensuremath{\mathbb{E}}[Z_n | Z_{n-1}=1] \\ &=& \frac{Z_{n-1} p_n N^d}{\prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i N^d} = W_{n-1}. \end{eqnarray*} The Martingale Convergence Theorem tells us that $W_n$ converges almost surely to a random variable $W$. Theorem 4.14 of \cite{Lyo} states that if \[ A:=\sup_{n} ||L_n ||_{\infty} < \infty, \] then $W>0$ a.s.\ given non-extinction. It is clearly the case that $A <\infty$, because $L_n$ can take at most the value $N^{d}$. Therefore, $W_n$ converges to a random variable $W$ which is stricly positive a.s.\ given non-extinction. The Lebesgue measure of the retained cubes at each iteration step $n$ is equal to $Z_n / N^{dn}$. We have \begin{equation} \lambda(\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}}^n) = \frac{Z_n}{N^{dn}} = \frac{\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i N^d \right) W_n}{N^{dn}} = \left(\prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i \right) W_n. \end{equation} Letting $n\to \infty$ in \eqref{eqn leb} yields $\lambda(\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}})= (\prod_{i=1}^{\infty}p_i) W$. Since $\prod_{i=1}^{\infty} p_i >0$ and $W>0$ a.s.\ given non-extinction, we get the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: Branching process in varying environment: the normalized count $W_n$ is a martingale with a.s. positive limit given survival (Lyons), so $\lambda(D_{fat})=(\prod p_i)W>0$.

nodes.name: Lebesgue measure of level-n set (3.18)
nodes.statement: \lambda(\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}}^n) = \frac{Z_n}{N^{dn}} = \frac{\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i N^d \right) W_n}{N^{dn}} = \left(\prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i \right) W_n.
nodes.label: eqn leb

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.8
nodes.statement: First, we have to introduce some notation. Let $U$ be the collection of points in $[0,1]^d$ not on the boundary of a subcube. For each $x\in U$ there exists a unique sequence $(C({\bf x}_1,\ldots,{\bf x}_n))_{n\geq 1}$ of cubes of the fractal process, where ${\bf x}_j\in J^d$ for all $j$, such that $\bigcap_{n\geq 1} C({\bf x}_1,\ldots,{\bf x}_n) = \{ x \}$. Therefore, we can define an invertible transformation $\phi : U \to (J^d)^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}}$ by $\phi(x) = ({\bf x}_1,{\bf x}_2,\ldots)$. For each $n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ let $\mu_n$ be the uniform measure on $(X_n,\ensuremath{\mathcal{F}}_n)$, where $X_n= J^d$ and $\ensuremath{\mathcal{F}}_n$ is the power set of $X_n$. Let $(X,\ensuremath{\mathcal{F}},\mu)=\bigotimes_{n=1}^{\infty}(X_n,\ensuremath{\mathcal{F}}_n,\mu_n)$ be the product space. Since $\phi : (U,\ensuremath{\mathcal{B}}(U),\lambda) \to (X,\ensuremath{\mathcal{F}},\mu)$ is an invertible measure-preserving transformation, we have that $(X,\ensuremath{\mathcal{F}},\mu)$ is by definition isomorphic to $(U,\ensuremath{\mathcal{B}}(U),\lambda)$. Here $\ensuremath{\mathcal{B}}(U)$ denotes the Borel $\sigma$-algebra. Next, we define the transformation $T:U\to U$, which will play a crucial role in the rest of the proof. Define the auxiliary shift transformation $T^* : X\to X$ by $T^*(({\bf x}_1,{\bf x}_2,{\bf x}_3,\ldots)) = ({\bf x}_2,{\bf x}_3,\ldots)$, for $({\bf x}_1,{\bf x}_2,\ldots)\in X$. The transformation $T^*$ is measure preserving with respect to the measure $\mu$ and also ergodic, see for instance \cite{Wal}. Let $T := \phi^{-1} \circ T^* \circ \phi$ be the induced transformation on $U$ and note that $T$ is isomorphic to $T^*$ and hence also ergodic. Informally, $T$ sends a point $x\in U$ to the point $Tx$, in such a way that the relative position of $Tx$ in the unit cube is the same as the relative position of $x$ in its level-1 cube $C({\bf x}_1)$; see Figure \ref{fig transformation}. \begin{figure}[!ht] \begin{center} \includegraphics[width=6cm]{transformation} \caption{Illustration of the transformation $T$. Note that the relative position of $x$ in the level-1 cube is the same as the relative position of $Tx$ in the unit cube.} \end{center} \end{figure} Recall that $\omega \in \Omega$ denotes a particular realization of the fat fractal percolation process. For $x \in U$, we define the following event. \[ A^x := \left\{\omega: \text{if we set } \omega(C(\textbf{x}_1,\ldots,\textbf{x}_n)) = 1 \text{ for all } n \geq 1, \text{ then } C_{\text{fat}}^{x} \neq \{x\} \right\}. \] In other words, $A^{x}$ consists of those configurations $\omega$ such that when we change the configuration by retaining all $C(\textbf{x}_1,\ldots,\textbf{x}_n)$, then in this new configuration, $x$ is in the same connected component as some $y \neq x$. Observe that \begin{equation} A^x \cap \{ x\in \ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}}\} =\{ x \in \ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}^{c}} \}. \end{equation} It is easy to see that $A^{x}$ is a tail event. Hence, by Kolmogorov's 0-1 law we get $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^{x}) \in \{0,1\}$ for all $x\in U$. However, a priori it is not clear that for almost all $x$ in the unit cube $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^x)$ has the same value. To this end, define the set $V:=\{x\in U: \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^{x})=0\}$. We will show that $\lambda(V)\in \{0,1\}$. Recall that the relative position of $Tx$ in the unit cube is the same as the relative position of $x$ in the level-1 cube $C(\mathbf{x}_1)$. It is possible to construct a coupling between the fractal process in the unit cube and the fractal process in $C(\mathbf{x}_1)$, given that $C(\mathbf{x}_1)$ is retained, with the following property: For every cube $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}})$ in $C(\mathbf{x}_1)$, it is the case that if $TC(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}})$ is retained in the fractal process in the unit cube, then $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}})$ is also retained in the fractal process in $C(\mathbf{x}_1)$, given that $C(\mathbf{x}_1)$ is retained. It is straightforward that such a coupling exists since the retention probabilities $p_n$ are non-decreasing in $n$. Hence, \begin{equation} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^{Tx}) \leq \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^x | C(\mathbf{x}_1) \text{ is retained}). \end{equation} Furthermore, since $A^x$ is a tail event, we have \begin{equation} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^x)=\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^x | C(\mathbf{x}_1) \text{ is retained}). \end{equation} It follows from \eqref{A^Tx ineq} and \eqref{cond eq} that $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^{Tx}) \leq \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^x)$ for all $x$. This implies that $V \subset T^{-1} V$. Because $T$ is measure preserving it follows that \[ \lambda(V \Delta T^{-1} V) = \lambda(V \setminus T^{-1}V) + \lambda(T^{-1}V \setminus V) = 0+\lambda(T^{-1}V) - \lambda(V) = 0. \] Ergodicity of $T$ now yields that $\lambda(V) \in \{0,1\}$. Suppose $\lambda(V)=0$. Then $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(x \in \ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}^{d}})=\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(\{x\in \ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}}\} \setminus A^x)=0$ for almost all $x\in [0,1]^d$, by \eqref{def A^x}. Applying Fubini's theorem gives \begin{eqnarray*} \ensuremath{\mathbb{E}} \lambda (\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}^{d}}) &=& \int_{\Omega}\int_{[0,1]^{d}} 1_{\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}^{d}}}(x,\omega)d\lambda d\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}} \\ &=& \int_{[0,1]^{d}}\int_{\Omega} 1_{\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}^{d}}}(x,\omega) d\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}} d\lambda\\ &=& \int_{[0,1]^{d}} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(x \in \ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}^{d}}) d\lambda = 0. \end{eqnarray*} Therefore $\lambda(\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}^{d}})=0$ a.s. By Theorem \ref{thm12} we have $\lambda(\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}^{c}})> 0$ a.s.\ given non-extinction. Next suppose that $\lambda(V)=1$. Then with a similar argument we can show that $\lambda(\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}^{c}})=0$ and $\lambda(\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}^{d}})>0$ a.s.\ given non-extinction.
nodes.statement_short: Ergodic-theory argument: conditional connectivity of $x$ is a tail event (0-1 law), and the ergodic shift $T$ forces its probability to be a.e. constant. Fubini then puts all measure on dust or on components.

nodes.name: A^x and non-dust points (3.19)
nodes.statement: A^x \cap \{ x\in \ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}}\} =\{ x \in \ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}^{c}} \}.
nodes.label: def A^x

nodes.name: Coupling inequality for A^{Tx} (3.20)
nodes.statement: \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^{Tx}) \leq \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^x | C(\mathbf{x}_1) \text{ is retained}).
nodes.label: A^Tx ineq

nodes.name: Tail-event conditioning (3.21)
nodes.statement: \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^x)=\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^x | C(\mathbf{x}_1) \text{ is retained}).
nodes.label: cond eq

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.9
nodes.statement_short: (i) union bound, translation invariance and FKG; (ii) Fubini on vertical segments plus Theorem 1.8; (iii) Borel-Cantelli.

nodes.name: Positive measure of full vertical lines (3.22)
nodes.statement: \lambda_{d-1}(\{x\in [0,1]^{d-1} : \{x\}\times [0,1] \subset \ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}} \}) > 0
nodes.label: strictly positive

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.11
nodes.statement: $(iii) \Rightarrow (ii)$. Trivial. $(ii) \Rightarrow (i)$. Suppose $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(x \mbox{ connected to } y) > 0$ for all $x,y \in U$, for some set $U\subset [0,1]^2$ with $\lambda(U) > 0$. Fix $y\in U$. By Fubini's theorem \begin{eqnarray*} \ensuremath{\mathbb{E}} \lambda(D^c_{\text{fat}}) &=& \int_{\Omega} \int_{[0,1]^2} 1_{D^c_{\text{fat}}}(x,\omega) d\lambda(x) d\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(\omega) \\ &=& \int_{[0,1]^2} \int_{\Omega} 1_{D^c_{\text{fat}}}(x,\omega) d\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(\omega) d\lambda(x) \\ &=& \int_{[0,1]^2} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(x\in D^c_{\text{fat}}) d\lambda(x) \\ &\geq& \int_{U\setminus \{y\}} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(x \mbox{ connected to } y) d\lambda(x) > 0. \end{eqnarray*} Hence $\lambda(D^c_{\text{fat}}) > 0$ with positive probability. By Theorem \ref{thm lebesgue} it follows that $\lambda(D^c_{\text{fat}}) > 0$ a.s.\ given non-extinction of the fat fractal process. $(i) \Rightarrow (iii)$. Next suppose that $\lambda(D^c_{\text{fat}}) > 0$ a.s.\ given non-extinction of the fat fractal process. For points $x\in[0,1]^2$ not on the boundary of a subcube, define the event $A^x$ as in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm lebesgue}. It follows from the proof of Theorem \ref{thm lebesgue} that $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^x)=1$ for all $x\in V$, for some set $V\subset[0,1]^2$ with $\lambda(V)=1$. By \eqref{def A^x} we have for all $x\in V$ \[ \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(x\in D^c_{\text{fat}})= \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(x\in D_{\text{fat}})>0. \] Let $x\in V$. Then \[ 0 < \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(x\in D^c_{\text{fat}}) \leq \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(\mbox{diam}(C^x_{\text{fat}}) > \textstyle{\frac{1}{n}}), \] where $\mbox{diam}(C^x_{\text{fat}})$ denotes the diameter of the set $C^x_{\text{fat}}$. So there exists a natural number $n_x$ such that $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(\mbox{diam}(C^x_{\text{fat}}) > \frac{1}{n_{x}}) > 0.$ Hence \[ \textstyle \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(x \mbox{ connected to } S(x,\frac{1}{2n_{x}})) > 0, \] where $S(x,\frac{1}{2n_{x}})$ is a circle centered at $x$ with radius $\frac{1}{2n_{x}}$. Write $x=(x_1,x_2)$ and define the following subsets of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^2$ \begin{eqnarray*} H_1 &=& \textstyle [0,1] \times [x_2-\frac{1}{4n_x},x_2], \\ H_2 &=& \textstyle [0,1] \times [x_2,x_2+\frac{1}{4n_x}], \\ V_1 &=& \textstyle [x_1-\frac{1}{4n_x},x_1] \times [0,1], \\ V_2 &=& \textstyle [x_1,x_1+\frac{1}{4n_x}] \times [0,1]. \end{eqnarray*} Note that for every $x \in [0,1]^2$ it is the case that at least one horizontal strip $H_i$ and at least one vertical strip $V_j$ is entirely contained in $[0,1]^2$. Define the event $\Gamma_x$ by \begin{eqnarray*} \Gamma_x &=& \bigcap_{i\in\{1,2\}:H_i \subset [0,1]^2} \{ \mbox{horizontal crossing in } H_i \} \\ &\cap& \bigcap_{j\in\{1,2\}:V_j \subset [0,1]^2}\{ \mbox{vertical crossing in } V_j \}. \end{eqnarray*} See Figure \ref{fig Gamma_x} for an illustration of the event $\Gamma_x$. From Theorem 2 in \cite{ChaChaDur} it follows that in the MFP model with parameter $p \geq p_c(N,2)$, the limit set $D_p$ connects the left-hand side of $[0,1]^2$ with its right-hand side with positive probability. It then follows from the RSW lemma (e.g.\ Lemma 5.1 in \cite{DekMee}) and the FKG inequality that $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{p}(\Gamma_x)>0$. Let $A_{n}$ denote the event of complete retention until level $n$, i.e.\ $\omega(C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}))=1$ for all $\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}} \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{J}}^{(n-1)}$. Since $\prod_{n=1}^{\infty} p_n >0$ there exists an integer $n_0$ such that $p_{n} \geq p_c(N,2)$ for all $n \geq n_0$. Hence, the probability measure $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{\text{fat}}(\cdot | A_{n_0}$) dominates $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{p_{c}(N,2)}(\cdot)$. Since $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{\text{fat}}(A_{n_0})>0$ it follows that $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{\text{fat}}(\Gamma_x) > 0$. \begin{figure}[!ht] \begin{center} \includegraphics[width=7cm]{Gamma_x} \caption{Realization of the event $\Gamma_x$.} \end{center} \end{figure} Observe that for $x,y \in V$ \begin{eqnarray*} \lefteqn{ \{ x \mbox{ connected to } y \} } \\ &\supset& \{ x \mbox{ connected to } S(x,\textstyle{\frac{1}{2n_x}}) \} \cap \Gamma_x \cap \{ y \mbox{ connected to } S(y,\textstyle{\frac{1}{2n_y}}) \} \cap \Gamma_y. \end{eqnarray*} Since all four events on the right-hand side are increasing and have positive probability, we can apply the FKG inequality to conclude that for all $x,y\in V$ we have $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(x \mbox{ connected to } y) > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Cycle of implications: Fubini plus Theorem 1.8 for (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i); for (i)$\Rightarrow$(iii), connect points to strip crossings using RSW, domination by critical MFP and FKG.

nodes.name: Fix delta and N_1
nodes.statement: Let $\delta>0$ and $N_0$ be such that $k(N)/N^d \leq p_0-2\delta =:p$ for all $N \geq N_0$. Choose $N_1 \geq N_0$ so large that $p_0/(4\delta^2 N^d) < \delta $ for $N \geq N_1$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose $\delta$, $N_0$, $N_1$.

nodes.name: Reduce to bound on E_m
nodes.statement: We will show that \begin{equation} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{p_{0}}(E_m) \geq 1-\frac{1}{4 \delta^2 N^{d}} , \end{equation} for all $m\geq 0$ and $N\geq N_1$. Since $E_m$ decreases to $E$ as $m\to\infty$, it follows that \[ \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{p_{0}}(E) = \lim_{m \to \infty} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{p_{0}}(E_m) \geq 1-\frac{1}{4 \delta^2 N^{d}}, \] for $N \geq N_1$. Now take $N_2\geq N_1$ so large that $1- \frac{1}{4 \delta^2 N^d} > 1- \epsilon$ for all $N \geq N_2$. It remains to show \eqref{induction E}.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce the lemma to the bound (2.6) on $P(E_m)$ via $E_m\downarrow E$.

nodes.name: Base case m=0
nodes.statement: We prove \eqref{induction E} by induction on $m$. Consider the event $E_0$, i.e.\ the event that the unit cube contains at least $k(N)$ retained level-1 subcubes. Let $X(n,p)$ denote a binomially distributed random variable with parameters $n\in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ and $p\in [0,1]$. Since the number of retained level-1 cubes has a binomial distribution with parameters $N^{d}$ and $p_0$, it follows from Chebyshev's inequality that, for every $N \geq N_1$, we have (writing $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}$ for the probability measure governing the binomially distributed random variables) \begin{eqnarray*} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{p_{0}}(E_0) &=& \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(X(N^d,p_0) \geq k(N)) \\ &\geq& \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(X(N^d,p_0) \geq p N^d) \\ &\geq& 1- \frac{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathbb{V}}\text{ar}} X(N^d,p_0)}{4\delta^2 N^{2d}} \\ &=& 1 -\frac{p_0(1-p_0)N^d}{4 \delta^2 N^{2d}} \\ &\geq& 1- \frac{1}{4 \delta^2 N^{d}}. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Base case via Chebyshev for Binomial$(N^d,p_0)$.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: Next, let $m\geq 0$ and $N \geq N_1$ and suppose that \eqref{induction E} holds for this $m$ and $N$. Recall that $E_{m+1}$ is the event that the unit cube contains at least $k(N)$ $m$-good level-1 cubes. The probability that a level-1 cube is $m$-good, given that it is retained, is equal to $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{p_0}(E_m)$. Using the induction hypothesis, we get \begin{eqnarray*} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{p_{0}}(E_{m+1}) &=& \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(X(N^{d},p_{0}\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{p_{0}}(E_m)) \geq k(N)) \\ & \geq& \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(X(N^d,p_0(1-\textstyle{\frac{1}{4 \delta^2 N^{d}}})) \geq k(N)). \end{eqnarray*} By our choices for $\delta$ and $N$ it follows that $p_0(1-\frac{1}{4 \delta^2 N^{d}}) > p+\delta$. Hence, using Chebyshev's inequality, we get \begin{eqnarray*} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(X(N^d,p_0(1-\textstyle{\frac{1}{4 \delta^2 N^{d}}})) \geq k(N)) &\geq&\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(X(N^d, p+\delta) \geq k(N)) \\ &\geq& \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(X(N^d, p+ \delta) \geq pN^d) \\ &\geq& 1- \frac{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathbb{V}}\text{ar}} X(N^d,p+\delta)}{\delta^2 N^{2d}} \\ &\geq& 1- \frac{1}{4\delta^2N^{d}}. \end{eqnarray*} Therefore, the induction step is valid and we have proved \eqref{induction E}.
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step: good children are binomial with parameter $p_0P(E_m)$; Chebyshev again.

nodes.name: Set up parameters and event E
nodes.statement: Let $p,p_0$ be such that $p < p_0 < \ensuremath{p_{c}(d)}$. Let $(k(N))_{N \geq 2}$ be a sequence such that $k(N)/N^d \leq p$, for all $N \geq 2$, and $k(N)/N^d \to p$ as $N \to \infty$. Consider an MFP model with parameters $p_0$ and $N$ and define the event $E$ as in \eqref{E}. Henceforth, we assume that $N$ is so large that $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{p_0}(E)>0$, which is possible by Lemma \ref{lem high prob}.
nodes.statement_short: Fix $p<p_0<p_c(d)$, $k(N)$ and the event $E$ with $P(E)>0$.

nodes.name: Coupling properties to construct
nodes.statement: In order to prove Theorem \ref{thm subcritical} we will use $E$ to construct two random subsets, $\tilde{D}_{p_{0}}$ and $\tilde{D}_{k(N)}$, of the unit cube, on a common probability space and with the following properties: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $\tilde{D}_{k(N)} \subset \tilde{D}_{p_{0}}$; \item[(ii)] the law of $\tilde{D}_{p_{0}}$ is stochastically dominated by the conditional law of $D_{p_{0}}$, conditioned on the event $E$; \item[(iii)] the law of $\tilde D_{k(N)}$ is the same as the law of $D_{k(N)}$.
nodes.statement_short: State the three coupling properties (i)-(iii) of the sets to construct.

nodes.name: Property (i)
nodes.statement: In order to prove Theorem \ref{thm subcritical} we will use $E$ to construct two random subsets, $\tilde{D}_{p_{0}}$ and $\tilde{D}_{k(N)}$, of the unit cube, on a common probability space and with the following properties: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $\tilde{D}_{k(N)} \subset \tilde{D}_{p_{0}}$;
nodes.statement_short: Inclusion property.

nodes.name: Property (ii)
nodes.statement: [(ii)] the law of $\tilde{D}_{p_{0}}$ is stochastically dominated by the conditional law of $D_{p_{0}}$, conditioned on the event $E$;
nodes.statement_short: Domination by the conditioned MFP law.

nodes.name: Property (iii)
nodes.statement: [(iii)] the law of $\tilde D_{k(N)}$ is the same as the law of $D_{k(N)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Correct marginal law of the $k$-model set.

nodes.name: Deduce the liminf bound
nodes.statement: It follows that the law of $D_{k(N)}$ is stochastically dominated by the conditional law of $D_{p_0}$, conditioned on the event $E$. Hence, the probability that the unit cube is crossed by $D_{k(N)}$ is at most the conditional probability that $D_{p_0}$ crosses the unit cube, conditioned on the event $E$. By \eqref{pc subcritical} the MFP process with parameter $p_0$ is subcritical, thus the latter probability equals zero. Using the fact that $k(N)/N^d \to p$ as $N \to \infty$, we conclude that \[ \liminf_{N \to \infty} \frac{k_{c}(N,d)}{N^{d}} \geq p. \] Since $p<\ensuremath{p_{c}(d)}$ was arbitrary, we get \[ \liminf_{N \to \infty} \frac{k_{c}(N,d)}{N^{d}} \geq \ensuremath{p_{c}(d)}. \]
nodes.statement_short: Domination plus subcriticality (2.4) give zero crossing probability, hence the liminf bound.

nodes.name: Reduce to the construction
nodes.statement: It remains to construct random sets $\tilde{D}_{p_{0}},\tilde{D}_{k(N)}$ with the properties (i)-(iii). First we construct two sequences $(\tilde{D}_{p_{0}}^n)_{n\geq 1}, (\tilde{D}_{k(N)}^n)_{n\geq 1}$ of decreasing random subsets.
nodes.statement_short: Remaining task: construct the coupled sets.

nodes.name: Law of number of infinity-good children
nodes.statement: Let ${\cal L}$ be the conditional law of the number of $\infty$-good level-1 cubes of the MFP process, conditioned on the event $E$. Note that the support of ${\cal L}$ is $\{k(N),k(N)+1,\ldots,N^d\}$. Furthermore, for a fixed level-$n$ cube $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}})$, ${\cal L}$ is also equal to the conditional law of the number of $\infty$-good level-$(n+1)$ subcubes in $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}})$, conditioned on $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}})$ being $\infty$-good.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the law $\mathcal{L}$ of the number of $\infty$-good children given $E$.

nodes.name: Iterative coupled construction
nodes.statement: Choose an integer $l$ according to ${\cal L}$ and choose $l$ level-1 cubes uniformly. Define $\tilde D_{p_0}^1$ as the closure of the union of these $l$ level-1 cubes. Choose $k(N)$ out of these $l$ cubes in a uniform way and define $\tilde D_{k(N)}^1$ as the closure of the union of these $k(N)$ cubes. For each level-1 cube $C({\bf I}) \subset \tilde D_{p_0}^1$, pick an integer $l({\bf I})$ according to ${\cal L}$, independently of other cubes, and choose $l({\bf I})$ level-2 subcubes of $C({\bf I})$ in a uniform way. Define $\tilde D_{p_0}^2$ as the closure of the union of all selected level-2 cubes. For each level-1 cube $C({\bf I}) \subset \tilde D_{k(N)}^1$, uniformly choose $k(N)$ out of the $l({\bf I})$ selected level-2 subcubes. Define $\tilde D_{k(N)}^2$ as the closure of the union of the $k(N)^2$ selected level-2 cubes of $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}})$. Iterating this procedure yields two infinite decreasing sequences of random subsets $(\tilde{D}_{p_{0}}^n)_{n\geq 1}, (\tilde{D}_{k(N)}^n)_{n\geq 1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Select $l\sim\mathcal{L}$ cubes, then $k(N)$ of them, recursively.

nodes.name: Limit sets satisfy (i)-(iii)
nodes.statement: Now define \[ \tilde D_{p_0} := \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} \tilde D_{p_0}^n,\quad \tilde D_{k(N)} := \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} \tilde D_{k(N)}^n. \] By construction, for each $n\geq 1$, we have that (1) $\tilde D_{k(N)}^n \subset \tilde D_{p_0}^n$, (2) the law of $\tilde{D}_{p_{0}}^n$ is stochastically dominated by the conditional law of $D_{p_{0}}^n$ given $E$ and (3) the law of $\tilde D_{k(N)}^n$ is equal to the law of $D_{k(N)}^n$. It follows that the limit sets $\tilde{D}_{p_{0}},\tilde{D}_{k(N)}$ satisfy properties (i)-(iii).
nodes.statement_short: Pass to the intersections; properties hold at every level and so in the limit.

nodes.name: Recursive claim
nodes.statement: Assume that the unit cube, i.e.\ $C(\emptyset)$, is $(n,u)$-good. We will show, with a recursive argument, that for $1\leq m \leq n$ there exists an edge-connected chain of retained $(n,u)$-good level-$m$ cubes which joins $\{0\} \times [0,1]^{d-1}$ and $\{1\} \times [0,1]^{d-1}$. In particular, this holds for $m=n$ and hence percolation occurs in $D_k^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to existence of good edge-connected chains at every level $m$.

nodes.name: Level 1 chain
nodes.statement: Since the unit cube is assumed to be $(n,u)$-good, $\ensuremath{\mathcal{D}}(\emptyset)$ contains by definition an edge-connected subset $\ensuremath{\mathcal{H}}(\emptyset)$ of retained $(n,u)$-good level-1 subcubes, such that each edge of $C(\emptyset)$ intersects at least $u$ cubes of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{H}}(\emptyset)$. In particular, there is a sequence of retained $(n,u)$-good edge-connected level-1 cubes that connects the left-hand side of $[0,1]^d$ with its right-hand side.
nodes.statement_short: Base: $\mathcal{H}(\emptyset)$ gives a level-1 chain.

nodes.name: Refine chain to next level
nodes.statement: Let $1\leq m < n$ and assume that there exists an edge-connected chain $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}_1),\ldots,C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}_l)$ of retained $(n,u)$-good level-$m$ cubes which connects the left-hand side of $[0,1]^d$ with its right-hand side. For each $i$, $1 \leq i \leq l$, either $\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}_i < \ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}_{i+1}$ or $\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}_{i+1}<\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}_i$. By condition (ii), there exist level-$(m+1)$ cubes of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{H}}(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}_{i+1})$ which are edge-connected to level-$(m+1)$ cubes of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{H}}(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}_i)$. These level-$(m+1)$ cubes $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{J}})$ are all $(n,u)$-good and have $Z_k(\ensuremath{\mathbf{J}})=1$, by \eqref{good subcubes} and the definition of the $\ensuremath{\mathcal{H}}(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}})$. It follows that there is an edge-connected chain of retained $(n,u)$-good level-$(m+1)$ cubes $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{J}})$ which joins $\{0\} \times [0,1]^{d-1}$ and $\{1\} \times [0,1]^{d-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Condition (ii) links $\mathcal{H}$ sets of consecutive chain cubes, giving a level-$(m+1)$ chain.

nodes.name: Reduce to conditional bound
nodes.statement: Fix $N \geq N_0$ and $n\geq 1$ and consider the $k(N)$-fractal model. Our aim is to show that \begin{equation} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{k(N)}(C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}) \text{ is } (n,u)\text{-good} \mid \ensuremath{\mathcal{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}^-)) \geq 1 -\epsilon \end{equation} holds for all $\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}} \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{J}}^{(n)}$. Taking $\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}=\emptyset$ then yields \eqref{unit cube good}. We prove this with a recursive argument.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to the conditional goodness bound (2.10) for every index.

nodes.name: Smallest index
nodes.statement: Let $\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}_0$ be the smallest index in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{J}}^{(n)}$, according to the ordering on $\ensuremath{\mathcal{J}}^{(n)}$. By virtue of the ordering, we have $|\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}_0| = n$. Hence, by definition, $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}_0)$ is $(n,u)$-good. In particular, \eqref{induction2} holds for $\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Base: the smallest index has level $n$ and is good by definition.

nodes.name: Recursive step
nodes.statement: The recursive step is as follows. Take an index $\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}} \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{J}}^{(n)}$ and assume that \begin{equation} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{k(N)}(C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}') \text{ is } (n,u)\text{-good} \mid \ensuremath{\mathcal{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}'^-)) \geq 1 -\epsilon, \end{equation} has been established for all indices $\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}'$ in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{J}}^{(n)}$ less than $\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}$. We have to show that \eqref{induction2} holds for $\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}$ given this assumption. We have two cases:
nodes.statement_short: Assume (2.11) for all smaller indices.

nodes.name: Case (a): level n
nodes.statement: [(a)] $|\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}| =n$; then $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{k(N)}(C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}) \text{ is } (n,u)\text{-good}) =1$ and \eqref{induction2} is true.
nodes.statement_short: Level-$n$ cubes are good by definition.

nodes.name: Case (b): lower level
nodes.statement: [(b)] $0 \leq |\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}| = m < n$.
nodes.statement_short: Opens the case of a cube of level $m<n$.

nodes.name: Good neighbours Q and sets U(I')
nodes.statement: For case (b), given $\ensuremath{\mathcal{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}^-)$, the goodness of $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}')$ is determined (in particular) for all $\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}' < \ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}$ with $|\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}|=m$. Let \begin{eqnarray*} \ensuremath{\mathcal{Q}}=\left\{\begin{array}{cc} \ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}': & \ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}'<\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}} \text{ and } C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}') \text{ is an } (n,u)\text{-good level-}m \\ & \text{ cube with an edge in common with }C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}) \end{array}\right\}. \end{eqnarray*} For each $\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}' \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{Q}}$, let $E(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}')$ be some common edge of $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}})$ and $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}')$. Since $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}')$ is $(n,u)$-good, there are at least $u$ level-$(m+1)$ subcubes in $\ensuremath{\mathcal{H}}(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}')$ which intersect $E(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}')$; call this set of subcubes $\ensuremath{\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}')$.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce earlier good neighbours $\mathcal{Q}$ and their boundary subcubes $\mathcal{U}(\mathbf{I}')$.

nodes.name: Apply induction hypothesis to children
nodes.statement: To see whether $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}})$ is $(n,u)$-good, we look at $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}},\ensuremath{\mathbf{j}}(l))$ where $\ensuremath{\mathbf{j}}(l), 1 \leq l \leq N^d,$ are the vectors of $J^d$ arranged in order. We have $(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}},\ensuremath{\mathbf{j}}(l)) < \ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}$, so by the induction hypothesis \eqref{induction} we have \begin{equation} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{k(N)}(C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}},\ensuremath{\mathbf{j}}(l)) \text{ is } (n,u)\text{-good} \mid \ensuremath{\mathcal{F}}((\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}},\ensuremath{\mathbf{j}}(l))^-)) \geq 1-\epsilon, \end{equation} for all $l$. Note that $\ensuremath{\mathcal{F}}((\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}},\ensuremath{\mathbf{j}}(1))^-) = \ensuremath{\mathcal{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}^-)$.
nodes.statement_short: Children precede $\mathbf{I}$, so the hypothesis gives (2.12).

nodes.name: Three coupled random sets
nodes.statement: We identify each subcube of $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}})$ in the canonical way with a vertex in $B_N$. We will construct three random subsets $G_1, G_2, G_3$ of $B_N$ on a common probability space with the following properties:
nodes.statement_short: Plan a coupling of three random subsets $G_1,G_2,G_3$ of $B_N$.

nodes.name: Property (I)
nodes.statement: [(I)] the law of $G_1$ equals the law of the set of subcubes $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}},\ensuremath{\mathbf{j}})$ of $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}})$ which are $(n,u)$-good and satisfy $Z_{k(N)}(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}},\ensuremath{\mathbf{j}})=1$;
nodes.statement_short: $G_1$ is the set of good retained children.

nodes.name: Property (II)
nodes.statement: [(II)] $G_2$ is obtained by first selecting $k(N)$ vertices of $B_N$ uniformly and then retaining each selected vertex with probability $1-\epsilon$, independently of other vertices;
nodes.statement_short: $G_2$ is a thinned uniform $k(N)$-set.

nodes.name: Properties (III)-(V)
nodes.statement: [(III)] the law of $G_3$ is the Bernoulli product measure with density $\pi$ on $B_N$; \item[(IV)] $G_1 \supset G_2$; \item[(V)] $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(G_2 \supset G_3) \geq 1-\epsilon/2$.
nodes.statement_short: $G_3$ is Bernoulli($\pi$), $G_1\supset G_2$, and $G_2\supset G_3$ with high probability.

nodes.name: Sequential coupling of G_1, G_2
nodes.statement: From \eqref{induction sub} and a standard coupling technique, sometimes referred to as sequential coupling (see e.g.\ \cite{LigSte}), the construction of $G_1$ and $G_2$ with properties (I), (II) and (IV) is straightforward.
nodes.statement_short: Sequential coupling from (2.12) gives $G_1\supset G_2$.

nodes.name: Construct G_3
nodes.statement: The construction of $G_3$ such that properties (III) and (V) hold is given below. Let $|G_2|$ denote the cardinality of the set $G_2$. Define $M=((1-\epsilon)p+\pi)N^d / 2$ and let $R$ be a number drawn from a binomial distribution with parameters $N^d$ and $\pi$, independently of $G_1$ and $G_2$. If $|G_2| \geq M$ and $M\geq R$ we select $R$ vertices uniformly out of the $|G_2|$ retained vertices of $G_2$ and call this set $G_3$. Otherwise, we select, independently of $G_1$ and $G_2$, $R$ vertices of $B_N$ in a uniform way and call this set $G_3$. From the construction (note that also $G_2$ was obtained in a uniform way) it is clear that $G_3$ satisfies property (III).
nodes.statement_short: Build $G_3$ from a Binomial$(N^d,\pi)$ count inside $G_2$ when possible.

nodes.name: Property (V) via Lemma 2.6
nodes.statement: Observe that $|G_2|$ has a binomial distribution with parameters $k(N)$ and $1-\epsilon$. From Lemma \ref{lem good3} it follows that \[ \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(\{|G_2| \geq M \} \cap \{R \leq M\}) \geq 1-\epsilon/2. \] Hence, property (V) also holds.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2.6 gives $|G_2|\ge M\ge R$ w.h.p., hence (V).

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 2.4 to G_3
nodes.statement: Let us now return to the goodness of $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}})$. As before, we identify the random subsets $G_1,G_2,G_3$ of $B_N$ with the corresponding sets of subcubes of $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}})$ in the canonical way. It then follows from property (III) and Lemma \ref{lem FalGri} (note that $\ensuremath{\mathcal{Q}}$ has cardinality at most $3^d =q$) that $G_3$ has an edge-connected subset which satisfies the following properties with probability at least $1-\epsilon/2$:
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 2.4 on the Bernoulli field $G_3$ yields an edge-connected subset with properties (i),(ii).

nodes.name: Property (i)
nodes.statement: [(i)] intersects every edge of $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}})$ with at least $u$ cubes;
nodes.statement_short: Meets each edge in $u$ cubes.

nodes.name: Property (ii)
nodes.statement: [(ii)] contains a cube that is edge-connected to a cube of $\ensuremath{\mathcal{U}}(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}')$, for all $\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}' \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{Q}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Links to each earlier good neighbour.

nodes.name: Combine bounds
nodes.statement: Combining properties (IV), (V) and the previous paragraph we obtain \begin{eqnarray*} \lefteqn{\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{k(N)}(C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}) \text{ is } (n,u)\text{-good} \mid \ensuremath{\mathcal{F}}(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}^-))} \\ & \geq& \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(\{G_1 \supset G_3 \} \cap \{G_3 \text{ satisfies properties (i) and (ii)}\}) \\ &\geq& 1-\epsilon. \end{eqnarray*} Therefore, \eqref{induction2} holds for the index $\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}$ given that \eqref{induction} holds for all indices $\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}'<\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Combine (IV), (V) and Lemma 2.4 to get conditional goodness $\ge 1-\epsilon$.

nodes.name: Iterate to the unit cube
nodes.statement: A recursive use of this argument -- recall that \eqref{induction2} is valid for $\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}_0$ (the smallest index according to the ordering) -- yields that \eqref{induction2} holds for all $\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}$. Taking $\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}=\emptyset$ in \eqref{induction2} proves the lemma.
nodes.statement_short: Recursion over all indices; take $\mathbf{I}=\emptyset$.

nodes.name: Level-n percolation bound
nodes.statement: Let $p>\ensuremath{p_{c}(d)}$ and consider a sequence $(k(N))_{N \geq 2}$ such that $k(N)/N^d \geq p$, for all $N \geq 2$. We get, using both Lemma \ref{lem prob} and Lemma \ref{lem good}, that for any $\epsilon >0$ such that $(1-\epsilon)p > \ensuremath{p_{c}(d)}$, there exists $N_0$, depending on $\epsilon$, such that \begin{equation} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{k(N)}(\text{percolation in } D^n_{k(N)}) \geq \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{k(N)}([0,1]^d \text{ is } (n,u)\text{-good}) \geq 1-\epsilon, \end{equation} for $N \geq N_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas 2.5 and 2.7 give percolation in $D^n_{k(N)}$ with probability $\ge 1-\epsilon$.

nodes.name: Pass to the limit set
nodes.statement: It is well known (see e.g.\ \cite{FalGri}) that \[ \{[0,1]^d \text{ is crossed by } D_{k(N)} \} = \bigcap_{n=1}^{\infty} \{\text{percolation in } D^n_{k(N)}\}. \] Hence, taking the limit $n\to \infty$ in \eqref{level percolation} yields that for $\epsilon > 0$ small enough \begin{equation} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{k(N)}([0,1]^d \text{ is crossed by } D_{k(N)}) \geq 1-\epsilon, \end{equation} for $N \geq N_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Crossing equals percolation at all levels; let $n\to\infty$.

nodes.name: Conclude theta tends to 1
nodes.statement: Therefore, \[ \theta(k(N),N,d) \to 1, \] as $N\to \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Hence $\theta(k(N),N,d)\to1$.

nodes.name: Proof strategy
nodes.statement: We use the idea of the proof of Theorem \ref{thm subcritical} and the result of Theorem \ref{thm supercritical}. Fix some $p_0$ such that $\ensuremath{p_{c}(d)}<p_0 < p$ and set $k(N):=\lfloor p_0 N^d \rfloor$. Consider the event $F$ that in the GFP model with generator $Y = Y(N,d)$ there exists an infinite tree of retained subcubes such that each subcube in the tree contains at least $k(N)$ retained subcubes in the tree. Similar to the proof of Lemma \ref{lem high prob}, we prove that $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(F)\to 1$ as $N\to\infty$. We then show that the law of $D_{k(N)}$ is stochastically dominated by the conditional law of $D_Y$, conditioned on the event $F$. By Theorem \ref{thm supercritical} we can then conclude that $\phi(Y(N,d),N,d) \to 1$ as $N \to \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Outline: event $F$ of an infinite good tree, domination, then Theorem 2.2.

nodes.name: m-good cubes and events F_m, F
nodes.statement: Consider the construction of $D_{Y}$. We will use the same definition of $m$-good as in Section \ref{sec subcritical}, that is, if a level-$n$ cube is retained and contains at least $k(N)$ retained subcubes, we call this level-$n$ cube 0-good. Recursively, we say that a level-$n$ cube is $(m+1)$-good if it is retained and contains at least $k(N)$ $m$-good level-$(n+1)$ subcubes. We call the unit cube $\infty$-good if it is $m$-good for every $m \geq 0$. Define the following events \begin{eqnarray*} F_m:=\{[0,1]^d \text{ is }m\text{-good}\},\\ F:=\{[0,1]^d \text{ is }\infty\text{-good}\}. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Reuse $m$-good with threshold $k(N)$ and define $F_m$, $F$.

nodes.name: Claim (2.15)
nodes.statement: We will show that for every $\epsilon>0$ such that $(1-\epsilon)p > p_0$ there exists $N_0=N_0(\epsilon)$ such that, for all $m \geq 0$, \begin{equation} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(F_m) > 1-\epsilon, \quad \text{for all } N \geq N_0 . \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Target: $P(F_m)>1-\epsilon$ uniformly in $m$.

nodes.name: Choose delta and N_0
nodes.statement: The proof of \eqref{claim m-good} is similar to the proof of Lemma \ref{lem high prob}. Let $\epsilon>0$ be such that $(1-\epsilon)p > p_0$. Take $\delta>0$ such that $(1-\epsilon)p>p_0+\delta$. Then, take $N_0$ so large that \begin{eqnarray} 1 - \frac{1}{4\delta^2 N} > 1-\epsilon/2 \quad \text{and} \\ \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(Y \geq p N^d) > 1-\epsilon/2 , \end{eqnarray} for all $N\geq N_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Pick $\delta$ and $N_0$ satisfying (2.16)-(2.17).

nodes.name: Base case F_0
nodes.statement: We prove that \eqref{claim m-good} holds for this $N_0$ and all $m\geq 0$, by induction on $m$. Since $k(N) = \lfloor p_0 N^d \rfloor \leq pN^d$ it follows from \eqref{Y bound} that $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(F_0)>1-\epsilon$, for all $N\geq N_0$.
nodes.statement_short: Base case from (2.17).

nodes.name: Inductive step for F_m
nodes.statement: Next, assume that \eqref{claim m-good} holds for some $m\geq 0$. The probability that a level-1 cube is $m$-good, given that it is retained, is equal to $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(F_m)$. It follows that, given that the number of retained level-1 cubes equals $y$, the number of $m$-good level-1 cubes has a binomial distribution with parameters $y$ and $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(F_m)$. By our choices for $N_0$ and $\delta$ we get \begin{eqnarray*} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(F_{m+1}) &=& \sum_{y \geq k(N)} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(X(y,\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(F_m)) \geq k(N)) \, \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(Y = y) \\ & \geq& \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(X(\lfloor pN^d \rfloor,\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(F_m)) \geq p_0 N^d) \, \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(Y \geq \lfloor pN^d \rfloor) \\ &\geq& \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(X(\lfloor pN^d \rfloor,1-\epsilon)\geq p_0 N^d) (1-\epsilon/2) \\ &\geq& \left(1-\frac{\ensuremath{\ensuremath{\mathbb{V}}\text{ar}} X(\lfloor pN^d \rfloor,1-\epsilon)}{(p_0 - (1-\epsilon)p)^2 N^{2d}}\right)(1-\epsilon/2) \\ &\geq& \left(1-\frac{(1-\epsilon)\epsilon pN^d}{\delta^2 N^{2d}}\right) (1-\epsilon/2) \\ &\geq& \left(1-\frac{1}{4 \delta^2 N^d}\right)(1-\epsilon/2) \\ &\geq& (1-\epsilon/2)(1-\epsilon/2)>1-\epsilon, \end{eqnarray*} for all $N \geq N_0$. Hence, the induction step is valid.
nodes.statement_short: Conditioned on $Y=y$, good children are binomial; Chebyshev bound.

nodes.name: Coupled sets, property (i)
nodes.statement: Analogously to the proof of Theorem \ref{thm subcritical} we use the event $F=\bigcap_{m=1}^{\infty} F_m$ to construct two random subsets $\tilde D_{k(N)}$ and $\tilde D_{Y}$ on a common probability space, with the following properties: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $\tilde{D}_{k(N)} \subset \tilde{D}_{Y}$;
nodes.statement_short: Construct coupled $\tilde D_{k(N)}\subset\tilde D_Y$.

nodes.name: Property (ii)
nodes.statement: [(ii)] the law of $\tilde{D}_{Y}$ is stochastically dominated by the conditional law of $D_{Y}$, conditioned on the event $F$;
nodes.statement_short: Domination by $D_Y$ given $F$.

nodes.name: Property (iii)
nodes.statement: [(iii)] the law of $\tilde D_{k(N)}$ is equal to the law of $D_{k(N)}$.
nodes.statement_short: Correct $k$-model law.

nodes.name: Construction as before
nodes.statement: This construction is the same (modulo replacing the binomial distribution with $Y$) as in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm subcritical} and is therefore omitted.
nodes.statement_short: Construction identical to that of Theorem 2.1.

nodes.name: Apply Theorem 2.2
nodes.statement: From properties (i)-(iii) and Theorem \ref{thm supercritical} we get \begin{eqnarray*} \lefteqn{\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}([0,1]^d \text{ is crossed by } D_{Y(N,d)} | F) } \\ &\geq& \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}([0,1]^d \text{ is crossed by } \tilde D_{Y(N,d)}) \\ &\geq & \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}([0,1]^d \text{ is crossed by } \tilde D_{k(N)}) \\ &=&\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}([0,1]^d \text{ is crossed by } D_{k(N)}) \to 1, \end{eqnarray*} as $N \to \infty$. Since \eqref{claim m-good} implies that $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(F) \to 1$ as $N \to \infty$, we obtain \[ \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}([0,1]^d \text{ is crossed by } D_{Y(N,d)}) \to 1, \] as $N \to \infty$.
nodes.statement_short: Domination and Theorem 2.2 give conditional crossing $\to1$; $P(F)\to1$ finishes.

nodes.name: Branching process Z_n
nodes.statement: Let $Z_n$ denote the number of retained level-$n$ cubes after iteration step $n$ and set $Z_0:=1$. Since the retention probabilities $p_n$ vary with $n$, the process $(Z_n)_{n \geq 1}$ is a so-called branching process in a time-varying environment. Following the notation of Lyons in \cite{Lyo} let $L_n$ be a random variable, having the distribution of $Z_n$ given that $Z_{n-1}=1$. Note that $L_n$ has a binomial distribution with parameters $N^{d}$ and $p_{n}$.
nodes.statement_short: View retained-cube counts as a branching process in a varying environment.

nodes.name: Normalized martingale W_n
nodes.statement: Define the process $(W_n)_{n \geq 1}$ by \[ W_n := \frac{Z_n}{\prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i N^d}. \] It is straightforward to show that $(W_n)_{n \geq 1}$ is a martingale: \begin{eqnarray*} \ensuremath{\mathbb{E}}[W_n | W_{n-1}] &=&\frac{\ensuremath{\mathbb{E}}[Z_n | Z_{n-1}]}{\prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i N^d} = \frac{Z_{n-1}}{\prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i N^d} \ensuremath{\mathbb{E}}[Z_n | Z_{n-1}=1] \\ &=& \frac{Z_{n-1} p_n N^d}{\prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i N^d} = W_{n-1}. \end{eqnarray*}
nodes.statement_short: Show $W_n=Z_n/\prod p_iN^d$ is a martingale.

nodes.name: Martingale convergence
nodes.statement: The Martingale Convergence Theorem tells us that $W_n$ converges almost surely to a random variable $W$.
nodes.statement_short: $W_n\to W$ a.s.

nodes.name: Lyons Theorem 4.14 gives W>0
nodes.statement: Theorem 4.14 of \cite{Lyo} states that if \[ A:=\sup_{n} ||L_n ||_{\infty} < \infty, \] then $W>0$ a.s.\ given non-extinction. It is clearly the case that $A <\infty$, because $L_n$ can take at most the value $N^{d}$. Therefore, $W_n$ converges to a random variable $W$ which is stricly positive a.s.\ given non-extinction.
nodes.statement_short: Lyons' criterion with offspring bounded by $N^d$ gives $W>0$ given survival.

nodes.name: Express Lebesgue measure through W
nodes.statement: The Lebesgue measure of the retained cubes at each iteration step $n$ is equal to $Z_n / N^{dn}$. We have \begin{equation} \lambda(\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}}^n) = \frac{Z_n}{N^{dn}} = \frac{\left(\prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i N^d \right) W_n}{N^{dn}} = \left(\prod_{i=1}^{n} p_i \right) W_n. \end{equation} Letting $n\to \infty$ in \eqref{eqn leb} yields $\lambda(\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}})= (\prod_{i=1}^{\infty}p_i) W$. Since $\prod_{i=1}^{\infty} p_i >0$ and $W>0$ a.s.\ given non-extinction, we get the desired result.
nodes.statement_short: $\lambda(D_{fat})=(\prod p_i)W>0$.

nodes.name: Symbolic coding of U
nodes.statement: First, we have to introduce some notation. Let $U$ be the collection of points in $[0,1]^d$ not on the boundary of a subcube. For each $x\in U$ there exists a unique sequence $(C({\bf x}_1,\ldots,{\bf x}_n))_{n\geq 1}$ of cubes of the fractal process, where ${\bf x}_j\in J^d$ for all $j$, such that $\bigcap_{n\geq 1} C({\bf x}_1,\ldots,{\bf x}_n) = \{ x \}$. Therefore, we can define an invertible transformation $\phi : U \to (J^d)^{\ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}}$ by $\phi(x) = ({\bf x}_1,{\bf x}_2,\ldots)$. For each $n \in \ensuremath{\mathbb{N}}$ let $\mu_n$ be the uniform measure on $(X_n,\ensuremath{\mathcal{F}}_n)$, where $X_n= J^d$ and $\ensuremath{\mathcal{F}}_n$ is the power set of $X_n$. Let $(X,\ensuremath{\mathcal{F}},\mu)=\bigotimes_{n=1}^{\infty}(X_n,\ensuremath{\mathcal{F}}_n,\mu_n)$ be the product space. Since $\phi : (U,\ensuremath{\mathcal{B}}(U),\lambda) \to (X,\ensuremath{\mathcal{F}},\mu)$ is an invertible measure-preserving transformation, we have that $(X,\ensuremath{\mathcal{F}},\mu)$ is by definition isomorphic to $(U,\ensuremath{\mathcal{B}}(U),\lambda)$. Here $\ensuremath{\mathcal{B}}(U)$ denotes the Borel $\sigma$-algebra.
nodes.statement_short: Code points of $U$ by their cube sequences; isomorphism with a product space.

nodes.name: Ergodic shift T
nodes.statement: Next, we define the transformation $T:U\to U$, which will play a crucial role in the rest of the proof. Define the auxiliary shift transformation $T^* : X\to X$ by $T^*(({\bf x}_1,{\bf x}_2,{\bf x}_3,\ldots)) = ({\bf x}_2,{\bf x}_3,\ldots)$, for $({\bf x}_1,{\bf x}_2,\ldots)\in X$. The transformation $T^*$ is measure preserving with respect to the measure $\mu$ and also ergodic, see for instance \cite{Wal}. Let $T := \phi^{-1} \circ T^* \circ \phi$ be the induced transformation on $U$ and note that $T$ is isomorphic to $T^*$ and hence also ergodic. Informally, $T$ sends a point $x\in U$ to the point $Tx$, in such a way that the relative position of $Tx$ in the unit cube is the same as the relative position of $x$ in its level-1 cube $C({\bf x}_1)$; see Figure \ref{fig transformation}.
nodes.statement_short: Define $T$ conjugate to the one-sided shift, hence measure preserving and ergodic.

nodes.name: Recall configuration
nodes.statement: Recall that $\omega \in \Omega$ denotes a particular realization of the fat fractal percolation process.
nodes.statement_short: Recall $\omega$.

nodes.name: Event A^x
nodes.statement: For $x \in U$, we define the following event. \[ A^x := \left\{\omega: \text{if we set } \omega(C(\textbf{x}_1,\ldots,\textbf{x}_n)) = 1 \text{ for all } n \geq 1, \text{ then } C_{\text{fat}}^{x} \neq \{x\} \right\}. \] In other words, $A^{x}$ consists of those configurations $\omega$ such that when we change the configuration by retaining all $C(\textbf{x}_1,\ldots,\textbf{x}_n)$, then in this new configuration, $x$ is in the same connected component as some $y \neq x$.
nodes.statement_short: Define the conditional-connectivity event $A^x$.

nodes.name: A^x and Kolmogorov 0-1 law
nodes.statement: Observe that \begin{equation} A^x \cap \{ x\in \ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}}\} =\{ x \in \ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}^{c}} \}. \end{equation} It is easy to see that $A^{x}$ is a tail event. Hence, by Kolmogorov's 0-1 law we get $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^{x}) \in \{0,1\}$ for all $x\in U$.
nodes.statement_short: On $x\in D_{fat}$, $A^x$ is $x\in D^c_{fat}$; $A^x$ is a tail event, so $P(A^x)\in\{0,1\}$.

nodes.name: Set V
nodes.statement: However, a priori it is not clear that for almost all $x$ in the unit cube $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^x)$ has the same value. To this end, define the set $V:=\{x\in U: \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^{x})=0\}$. We will show that $\lambda(V)\in \{0,1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $V=\{x:P(A^x)=0\}$; aim $\lambda(V)\in\{0,1\}$.

nodes.name: Recall relative position
nodes.statement: Recall that the relative position of $Tx$ in the unit cube is the same as the relative position of $x$ in the level-1 cube $C(\mathbf{x}_1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall the geometric meaning of $T$.

nodes.name: Monotone coupling
nodes.statement: It is possible to construct a coupling between the fractal process in the unit cube and the fractal process in $C(\mathbf{x}_1)$, given that $C(\mathbf{x}_1)$ is retained, with the following property: For every cube $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}})$ in $C(\mathbf{x}_1)$, it is the case that if $TC(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}})$ is retained in the fractal process in the unit cube, then $C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}})$ is also retained in the fractal process in $C(\mathbf{x}_1)$, given that $C(\mathbf{x}_1)$ is retained. It is straightforward that such a coupling exists since the retention probabilities $p_n$ are non-decreasing in $n$. Hence, \begin{equation} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^{Tx}) \leq \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^x | C(\mathbf{x}_1) \text{ is retained}). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Non-decreasing $p_n$ give a coupling and inequality (3.20).

nodes.name: Tail conditioning
nodes.statement: Furthermore, since $A^x$ is a tail event, we have \begin{equation} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^x)=\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^x | C(\mathbf{x}_1) \text{ is retained}). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Conditioning on the first cube does not change $P(A^x)$.

nodes.name: V subset of preimage
nodes.statement: It follows from \eqref{A^Tx ineq} and \eqref{cond eq} that $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^{Tx}) \leq \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^x)$ for all $x$. This implies that $V \subset T^{-1} V$.
nodes.statement_short: $P(A^{Tx})\le P(A^x)$, so $V\subset T^{-1}V$.

nodes.name: Ergodicity
nodes.statement: Because $T$ is measure preserving it follows that \[ \lambda(V \Delta T^{-1} V) = \lambda(V \setminus T^{-1}V) + \lambda(T^{-1}V \setminus V) = 0+\lambda(T^{-1}V) - \lambda(V) = 0. \] Ergodicity of $T$ now yields that $\lambda(V) \in \{0,1\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Invariance mod null sets and ergodicity give $\lambda(V)\in\{0,1\}$.

nodes.name: Case lambda(V)=0
nodes.statement: Suppose $\lambda(V)=0$. Then $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(x \in \ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}^{d}})=\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(\{x\in \ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}}\} \setminus A^x)=0$ for almost all $x\in [0,1]^d$, by \eqref{def A^x}. Applying Fubini's theorem gives \begin{eqnarray*} \ensuremath{\mathbb{E}} \lambda (\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}^{d}}) &=& \int_{\Omega}\int_{[0,1]^{d}} 1_{\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}^{d}}}(x,\omega)d\lambda d\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}} \\ &=& \int_{[0,1]^{d}}\int_{\Omega} 1_{\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}^{d}}}(x,\omega) d\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}} d\lambda\\ &=& \int_{[0,1]^{d}} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(x \in \ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}^{d}}) d\lambda = 0. \end{eqnarray*} Therefore $\lambda(\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}^{d}})=0$ a.s. By Theorem \ref{thm12} we have $\lambda(\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}^{c}})> 0$ a.s.\ given non-extinction.
nodes.statement_short: Fubini gives null dust; Theorem 1.7 gives positive connected measure.

nodes.name: Case lambda(V)=1
nodes.statement: Next suppose that $\lambda(V)=1$. Then with a similar argument we can show that $\lambda(\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}^{c}})=0$ and $\lambda(\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}^{d}})>0$ a.s.\ given non-extinction.
nodes.statement_short: Symmetric argument.

nodes.name: Part (i)
nodes.statement: (i) Suppose that $\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}}$ has a non-empty interior with positive probability. Then we have \begin{eqnarray*} 0 &<& \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}} \text{ has non-empty interior}) \\ &=& \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(\exists n, \exists \ensuremath{\mathbf{i}}_1,\ldots,\ensuremath{\mathbf{i}}_n: C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{i}}_1,\ldots,\ensuremath{\mathbf{i}}_n) \subset \ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}}) \\ &\leq& \sum_{ n, \ensuremath{\mathbf{i}}_1,\ldots,\ensuremath{\mathbf{i}}_n} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{i}}_1,\ldots,\ensuremath{\mathbf{i}}_n) \subset \ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}}). \end{eqnarray*} Since we sum over countably many cubes, there must exist $n$ and $\ensuremath{\mathbf{i}}_1,\ldots,\ensuremath{\mathbf{i}}_n$ such that $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{i}}_1,\ldots,\ensuremath{\mathbf{i}}_n) \subset \ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}}) > 0$. Hence, by translation invariance, $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{i}}_1,\ldots,\ensuremath{\mathbf{i}}_n) \subset \ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}}) > 0$ for this specific $n$ and all $\ensuremath{\mathbf{i}}_1,\ldots,\ensuremath{\mathbf{i}}_n$. We can apply the FKG inequality to obtain $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}} = [0,1]^d) = \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{i}}_1,\ldots,\ensuremath{\mathbf{i}}_n) \subset \ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}} \,\forall \ensuremath{\mathbf{i}}_1,\ldots,\ensuremath{\mathbf{i}}_n) >0$. Since $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}} = [0,1]^d) = \prod_{n=1}^{\infty} p_n^{N^{dn}}$, this proves the first part of the theorem.
nodes.statement_short: Union bound, translation invariance and FKG: positive chance of full cube.

nodes.name: Part (ii)
nodes.statement_short: Fubini over vertical segments gives positive connected measure; apply Theorem 1.8.

nodes.name: Part (iii)
nodes.statement: (iii) Next assume that $\prod_{n=1}^{\infty} p_n^{N^{dn}} > 0$. For each level $n$, we have $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}}^n=\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}}^{n-1}) \geq p_n^{N^{dn}}$. Since $\prod_{n=1}^{\infty} p_n^{N^{dn}} > 0$ is equivalent to $\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}( 1 - p_n^{N^{dn}}) < \infty$, we have \[ \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}}^n\neq \ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}}^{n-1}) \leq \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} (1 - p_n^{N^{dn}}) < \infty. \] Applying the Borel-Cantelli lemma gives that, with probability 1, $\{\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}}^n \neq \ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}}^{n-1}\}$ occurs for only finitely many $n$. Hence, with probability 1 there exists an $n$ such that $\ensuremath{D_{\text{fat}}}$ can be written as the union of level-$n$ cubes.
nodes.statement_short: Borel-Cantelli: only finitely many levels lose cubes.

nodes.name: (iii) implies (ii) implies (i)
nodes.statement: $(iii) \Rightarrow (ii)$. Trivial. $(ii) \Rightarrow (i)$. Suppose $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(x \mbox{ connected to } y) > 0$ for all $x,y \in U$, for some set $U\subset [0,1]^2$ with $\lambda(U) > 0$. Fix $y\in U$. By Fubini's theorem \begin{eqnarray*} \ensuremath{\mathbb{E}} \lambda(D^c_{\text{fat}}) &=& \int_{\Omega} \int_{[0,1]^2} 1_{D^c_{\text{fat}}}(x,\omega) d\lambda(x) d\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(\omega) \\ &=& \int_{[0,1]^2} \int_{\Omega} 1_{D^c_{\text{fat}}}(x,\omega) d\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(\omega) d\lambda(x) \\ &=& \int_{[0,1]^2} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(x\in D^c_{\text{fat}}) d\lambda(x) \\ &\geq& \int_{U\setminus \{y\}} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(x \mbox{ connected to } y) d\lambda(x) > 0. \end{eqnarray*} Hence $\lambda(D^c_{\text{fat}}) > 0$ with positive probability. By Theorem \ref{thm lebesgue} it follows that $\lambda(D^c_{\text{fat}}) > 0$ a.s.\ given non-extinction of the fat fractal process.
nodes.statement_short: (iii)$\Rightarrow$(ii) is trivial; for (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i), Fubini gives $E\lambda(D^c)>0$ and Theorem 1.8 upgrades to a.s.

nodes.name: (i) implies (iii)
nodes.statement: $(i) \Rightarrow (iii)$. Next suppose that $\lambda(D^c_{\text{fat}}) > 0$ a.s.\ given non-extinction of the fat fractal process. For points $x\in[0,1]^2$ not on the boundary of a subcube, define the event $A^x$ as in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm lebesgue}. It follows from the proof of Theorem \ref{thm lebesgue} that $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(A^x)=1$ for all $x\in V$, for some set $V\subset[0,1]^2$ with $\lambda(V)=1$. By \eqref{def A^x} we have for all $x\in V$ \[ \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(x\in D^c_{\text{fat}})= \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(x\in D_{\text{fat}})>0. \] Let $x\in V$. Then \[ 0 < \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(x\in D^c_{\text{fat}}) \leq \sum_{n=1}^{\infty} \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(\mbox{diam}(C^x_{\text{fat}}) > \textstyle{\frac{1}{n}}), \] where $\mbox{diam}(C^x_{\text{fat}})$ denotes the diameter of the set $C^x_{\text{fat}}$. So there exists a natural number $n_x$ such that $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(\mbox{diam}(C^x_{\text{fat}}) > \frac{1}{n_{x}}) > 0.$ Hence \[ \textstyle \ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(x \mbox{ connected to } S(x,\frac{1}{2n_{x}})) > 0, \] where $S(x,\frac{1}{2n_{x}})$ is a circle centered at $x$ with radius $\frac{1}{2n_{x}}$. Write $x=(x_1,x_2)$ and define the following subsets of $\ensuremath{\mathbb{R}}^2$ \begin{eqnarray*} H_1 &=& \textstyle [0,1] \times [x_2-\frac{1}{4n_x},x_2], \\ H_2 &=& \textstyle [0,1] \times [x_2,x_2+\frac{1}{4n_x}], \\ V_1 &=& \textstyle [x_1-\frac{1}{4n_x},x_1] \times [0,1], \\ V_2 &=& \textstyle [x_1,x_1+\frac{1}{4n_x}] \times [0,1]. \end{eqnarray*} Note that for every $x \in [0,1]^2$ it is the case that at least one horizontal strip $H_i$ and at least one vertical strip $V_j$ is entirely contained in $[0,1]^2$. Define the event $\Gamma_x$ by \begin{eqnarray*} \Gamma_x &=& \bigcap_{i\in\{1,2\}:H_i \subset [0,1]^2} \{ \mbox{horizontal crossing in } H_i \} \\ &\cap& \bigcap_{j\in\{1,2\}:V_j \subset [0,1]^2}\{ \mbox{vertical crossing in } V_j \}. \end{eqnarray*} See Figure \ref{fig Gamma_x} for an illustration of the event $\Gamma_x$. From Theorem 2 in \cite{ChaChaDur} it follows that in the MFP model with parameter $p \geq p_c(N,2)$, the limit set $D_p$ connects the left-hand side of $[0,1]^2$ with its right-hand side with positive probability. It then follows from the RSW lemma (e.g.\ Lemma 5.1 in \cite{DekMee}) and the FKG inequality that $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{p}(\Gamma_x)>0$. Let $A_{n}$ denote the event of complete retention until level $n$, i.e.\ $\omega(C(\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}}))=1$ for all $\ensuremath{\mathbf{I}} \in \ensuremath{\mathcal{J}}^{(n-1)}$. Since $\prod_{n=1}^{\infty} p_n >0$ there exists an integer $n_0$ such that $p_{n} \geq p_c(N,2)$ for all $n \geq n_0$. Hence, the probability measure $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{\text{fat}}(\cdot | A_{n_0}$) dominates $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{p_{c}(N,2)}(\cdot)$. Since $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{\text{fat}}(A_{n_0})>0$ it follows that $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}_{\text{fat}}(\Gamma_x) > 0$. \begin{figure}[!ht] \begin{center} \includegraphics[width=7cm]{Gamma_x} \caption{Realization of the event $\Gamma_x$.} \end{center} \end{figure} Observe that for $x,y \in V$ \begin{eqnarray*} \lefteqn{ \{ x \mbox{ connected to } y \} } \\ &\supset& \{ x \mbox{ connected to } S(x,\textstyle{\frac{1}{2n_x}}) \} \cap \Gamma_x \cap \{ y \mbox{ connected to } S(y,\textstyle{\frac{1}{2n_y}}) \} \cap \Gamma_y. \end{eqnarray*} Since all four events on the right-hand side are increasing and have positive probability, we can apply the FKG inequality to conclude that for all $x,y\in V$ we have $\ensuremath{\mathbb{P}}(x \mbox{ connected to } y) > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Connect points to strip crossings and glue with FKG.
